title: Introduction to Causal ML in R
text:
Machine learning is very good at prediction. It can tell us who is likely to churn, which loan may default, or which student may score poorly on an exam. But many real decisions are not prediction questions. They are intervention questions.
Suppose you are deciding whether to offer tutoring to a student. The real question is not “Who tends to score well?” The real question is “How much would this student’s score change if they received tutoring?”
That is a causal question.

title: Introduction to Causal ML in R
text:
Prediction Is Not Causation
If we look at historical data, we may notice that students who received tutoring scored lower on average than students who did not. A predictive model could learn that tutoring is associated with lower scores.
That does not mean tutoring hurts students.
It may simply be that struggling students were more likely to receive tutoring in the first place. This is called confounding. A confounder is a variable that affects both treatment assignment and the outcome.
In this example:

Students with low baseline scores may be more likely to get tutoring.
Those same students may also have lower future scores, even after extra help.

So the raw comparison is unfair.

title: Introduction to Causal ML in R
section: What Causal ML Tries to Estimate
text:
What Causal ML Tries to Estimate
The central idea in causal inference is the counterfactual.
For each person, we want to compare two worlds:

What would happen if they received the treatment?
What would happen if they did not?

Of course, we only get to observe one of those worlds. Causal methods try to recover the missing one as carefully as possible.
At a high level, causal ML combines two ideas:

Causal inference gives the framework for asking intervention questions correctly.
Machine learning helps model complex patterns, especially when treatment effects are not the same for everyone.

title: Introduction to Causal ML in R
text:
Why Causal ML Is Needed
Classical causal tools such as randomized experiments and regression are extremely important. But modern decision problems are often more complicated:

There may be many confounding variables.
Relationships may be non-linear.
The treatment may help some people much more than others.
We may want to personalize decisions rather than estimate one average effect.

Causal ML is useful when we want to estimate effects like:

Which customers will respond most to a marketing offer?
Which patients benefit most from a treatment?
Which students gain most from tutoring?

The key point is simple: standard ML predicts outcomes, while causal ML tries to estimate the effect of an action.

title: Introduction to Causal ML in R
text:
A Simple Example in R
We will simulate data for a tutoring program. In our synthetic world:

students have a baseline test score,
students study for different numbers of hours,
some students are more motivated than others,
weaker students are more likely to receive tutoring,
tutoring helps, but it helps weaker students more.

This setup is useful because we know the true treatment effect in the simulated data. That lets us compare naive analysis with better causal analysis.

set.seed(42)

n <- 1500

students <- data.frame(
  pretest = pmin(100, pmax(30, round(rnorm(n, mean = 68, sd = 12)))),
  study_hours = pmax(0, round(rnorm(n, mean = 6, sd = 2), 1)),
  motivation = runif(n, min = 0, max = 1)
)

# Students with lower pretest scores are more likely to be assigned tutoring.
log_odds_treat <- 2.5 - 0.04 * students$pretest + 0.8 * students$motivation
prob_treat <- plogis(log_odds_treat)
students$treat <- rbinom(n, size = 1, prob = prob_treat)

# True treatment effect is larger for weaker students.
students$true_tau <- 12 - 0.10 * students$pretest + 2 * students$motivation

students$posttest <- 35 +
  0.55 * students$pretest +
  1.8 * students$study_hours +
  6 * students$motivation +
  students$treat * students$true_tau +
  rnorm(n, mean = 0, sd = 5)

head(students)

  pretest study_hours motivation treat true_tau posttest
1      84         4.8 0.24646324     1 4.092926 94.39913
2      61         5.7 0.53030519     1 6.960610 82.88053
3      72         4.0 0.21397210     0 5.227944 82.98620
4      76         7.7 0.02584904     0 4.451698 87.04493
5      73         4.4 0.34200247     0 5.384005 91.06745
6      67         6.7 0.39413527     1 6.088271 99.91392

title: Introduction to Causal ML in R
text:
Step 1: The Naive Comparison
Let us compare average post-test scores for tutored and non-tutored students.

tapply(students$posttest, students$treat, mean)

       0        1 
87.10406 91.76007 

naive_effect <- with(students,
  mean(posttest[treat == 1]) - mean(posttest[treat == 0])
)

naive_effect

[1] 4.656002


This difference is easy to compute, but it mixes together two things:

the effect of tutoring,
the fact that struggling students were more likely to receive tutoring.

Now compare the baseline scores of the two groups.

tapply(students$pretest, students$treat, mean)

       0        1 
70.46565 65.40473 


If the tutored group starts from a weaker baseline, then a raw comparison is not an apples-to-apples comparison.

title: Introduction to Causal ML in R
section: Step 2: What Is the True Average Effect?
text:
Step 2: What Is the True Average Effect?
Because we simulated the data, we actually know the true treatment effect for each student.

true_ate <- mean(students$true_tau)
true_ate

[1] 6.228336


In real life, we do not know this number. But in a simulation it is a helpful benchmark.

title: Introduction to Causal ML in R
text:
Step 3: A Simple Regression Adjustment
A first causal step is to adjust for observed confounders. This is not yet “causal ML” in the modern sense, but it is an important baseline.

lm_fit <- lm(posttest ~ treat + pretest + study_hours + motivation, data = students)
summary(lm_fit)$coefficients

              Estimate Std. Error  t value      Pr(>|t|)
(Intercept) 37.7458376 0.92990797 40.59094 1.873577e-243
treat        6.4573821 0.27542075 23.44552 8.890104e-104
pretest      0.4925642 0.01146321 42.96915 2.269745e-263
study_hours  1.8766798 0.06490833 28.91277 2.240400e-146
motivation   7.5710141 0.45894933 16.49641  2.691824e-56


The coefficient on treat is now comparing students with similar baseline characteristics instead of mixing everyone together.

title: Introduction to Causal ML in R
section: Step 4: A Simple Causal ML Idea
text:
Step 4: A Simple Causal ML Idea
One common idea in causal ML is to estimate two models:

one model for the treated group,
one model for the control group.

Then for each student we predict:

expected score if treated,
expected score if not treated,

and subtract the two predictions. This is sometimes called a T-learner.
We will use decision trees to keep the code approachable.

library(rpart)

treated_model <- rpart(
  posttest ~ pretest + study_hours + motivation,
  data = students[students$treat == 1, ],
  method = "anova",
  control = rpart.control(cp = 0.01, minsplit = 30)
)

control_model <- rpart(
  posttest ~ pretest + study_hours + motivation,
  data = students[students$treat == 0, ],
  method = "anova",
  control = rpart.control(cp = 0.01, minsplit = 30)
)

students$mu1_hat <- predict(treated_model, newdata = students)
students$mu0_hat <- predict(control_model, newdata = students)
students$tau_hat <- students$mu1_hat - students$mu0_hat

head(students[, c("pretest", "motivation", "true_tau", "tau_hat")])

  pretest motivation true_tau   tau_hat
1      84 0.24646324 4.092926  6.132321
2      61 0.53030519 6.960610 10.674708
3      72 0.21397210 5.227944  3.464018
4      76 0.02584904 4.451698  2.585313
5      73 0.34200247 5.384005  6.132321
6      67 0.39413527 6.088271  6.453480


This gives an estimated treatment effect for each student, not just one overall average.

title: Introduction to Causal ML in R
text:
Who Benefits the Most?
Now let us look at estimated treatment effects by baseline score band.

students$score_band <- cut(
  students$pretest,
  breaks = c(30, 50, 65, 80, 100),
  include.lowest = TRUE
)

aggregate(cbind(true_tau, tau_hat) ~ score_band, data = students, mean)

  score_band true_tau  tau_hat
1    [30,50] 8.486052 7.586667
2    (50,65] 7.053347 6.644504
3    (65,80] 5.766436 7.026083
4   (80,100] 4.347571 5.490518


You should see a pattern where lower-scoring students tend to benefit more from tutoring. That is called heterogeneous treatment effects. In many real applications, this is exactly what decision-makers want to know.

title: Introduction to Causal ML in R
text:
Visualizing Estimated Effects

plot(
  students$pretest,
  students$tau_hat,
  pch = 16,
  col = rgb(0.1, 0.4, 0.7, 0.25),
  xlab = "Pre-test score",
  ylab = "Estimated tutoring effect",
  main = "Estimated Treatment Effect by Baseline Score"
)

lines(
  lowess(students$pretest, students$tau_hat, f = 0.4),
  col = "firebrick",
  lwd = 3
)








The smooth line helps show how the estimated effect changes across students. In this simulation, the estimated effect should generally decline as the pre-test score rises.

title: Introduction to Causal ML in R
section: Why This Is Still Only a Starting Point
text:
Why This Is Still Only a Starting Point
This example is useful for intuition, but real causal ML is more careful than this simple workflow.
In practice, analysts often use methods such as:

causal forests,
doubly robust learners,
meta-learners such as the T-learner, S-learner, and X-learner,
uplift models for treatment targeting.

They also worry about assumptions such as:

no important unobserved confounders,
enough overlap between treated and untreated groups,
correct measurement of treatment and outcome.

No algorithm can fully fix bad data or a broken study design.

title: Introduction to Causal ML in R
text:
A Few Takeaways

Causal questions ask what would happen under different actions.
Predictive ML alone cannot answer causal questions.
Confounding can make naive comparisons misleading.
Causal ML is especially useful when treatment effects vary across people.
In R, even a simple simulation can help build intuition for counterfactual thinking.

title: Introduction to Causal ML in R
text:
One More Useful Check
Since this is simulated data, we can compare the average estimated effect with the true average effect.

c(
  naive = naive_effect,
  regression_adjusted = coef(lm_fit)["treat"],
  t_learner_average = mean(students$tau_hat),
  true_ate = true_ate
)

                    naive regression_adjusted.treat         t_learner_average 
                 4.656002                  6.457382                  6.719138 
                 true_ate 
                 6.228336 


This comparison is a nice reminder that causal estimation is about recovering the effect of an intervention, not just finding correlations in the observed data.
If you want to extend this example, try changing the data-generating process:

make treatment almost random,
add stronger confounding,
make the treatment effect non-linear,
remove one important confounder and see what happens.

That kind of experimentation is one of the fastest ways to develop intuition for causal ML.

title: Using Causal ML to Answer Credit Risk Questions
text:
Most credit risk models are built to answer predictive questions such as: “Who is likely to default?” Causal questions are different. They ask what will happen if we take an action.
Examples in credit risk management include:
Causal ML helps answer these questions by estimating treatment effects rather than just predicting outcomes.

title: Using Causal ML to Answer Credit Risk Questions
text:
Start with the causal question
Before choosing a model, define the business decision in plain language.
For example:

Treatment: customer receives a proactive collections call within 7 days of missing a payment.
Outcome: customer cures within 30 days, or avoids charge-off within 12 months.
Estimand: average treatment effect, or treatment effect for specific borrower segments.

That framing matters because causal ML is only useful when treatment, outcome, and timing are all clearly defined.

title: Using Causal ML to Answer Credit Risk Questions
text:
Why prediction is not enough
A standard machine learning model can tell you which borrowers look risky. It usually cannot tell you whether an intervention caused a better outcome.
Suppose collectors tend to call the riskiest borrowers first. If those borrowers later default at a high rate, a naive analysis may conclude that calls are ineffective. In reality, the calls may still have reduced losses relative to what would have happened otherwise.
This is the core problem causal ML tries to solve: estimating the counterfactual.

title: Using Causal ML to Answer Credit Risk Questions
section: A practical workflow for credit risk teams
text:
A practical workflow for credit risk teams
The workflow is usually:

Identify the intervention and outcome.
Assemble pre-treatment features that influence both treatment assignment and outcome.
Estimate treatment effects using a causal model.
Validate whether the estimated uplift is stable and decision-useful.
Deploy policy rules around who should receive the intervention.

In credit risk, useful pre-treatment features often include bureau variables, utilization, delinquency history, income proxies, product type, tenure, prior contact history, and macro context available at decision time.
The phrase “pre-treatment” is important. Do not include variables created after the intervention, because that leaks the effect you are trying to measure.

title: Using Causal ML to Answer Credit Risk Questions
text:
Where causal ML fits
Common causal ML methods include:

T-learners and X-learners for flexible treatment effect estimation.
Doubly robust methods that combine outcome and propensity models.
Causal forests for heterogeneous treatment effects.

For many applied credit risk questions, causal forests are a useful starting point because they can capture non-linear effects and highlight which customer segments benefit most from an action.

title: Using Causal ML to Answer Credit Risk Questions
text:
Simple example in R
Assume we have historical data at the borrower level:

treatment: whether a collections call was made.
outcome: whether the account cured within 30 days.
X: borrower characteristics known before the call decision.

The goal is to estimate which borrowers are most likely to benefit from the call.
library(grf)

# treatment: 1 if borrower received a collections call
# outcome: 1 if borrower cured within 30 days
# X: pre-treatment borrower features

causal_fit <- causal_forest(
  X = borrower_features,
  Y = cure_30d,
  W = treatment_flag
)

tau_hat <- predict(causal_fit)$predictions

head(tau_hat)
tau_hat is the estimated treatment effect for each borrower. A higher value means the model expects a larger improvement in cure rate if that borrower receives the intervention.
You can then rank customers by expected uplift rather than by raw default risk.
borrower_scored <- data.frame(
  borrower_id = borrower_id,
  uplift = tau_hat
)

borrower_scored <- borrower_scored[order(-borrower_scored$uplift), ]

head(borrower_scored, 10)
This changes the operational question from “Who is risky?” to “Who is most likely to improve because we act?”

title: Using Causal ML to Answer Credit Risk Questions
section: Example use cases in credit risk management
text:
Example use cases in credit risk management
Here are a few strong applications:

Collections optimization: estimate which delinquent borrowers are most likely to cure if contacted.
Credit line management: identify customers whose line increases create incremental spend without disproportionate loss.
Hardship strategy: determine which distressed borrowers benefit from restructuring versus standard collections.
Pricing and offers: evaluate whether a retention offer or repricing action changes attrition and future profitability.

In each case, the target is not just risk prediction. It is incremental impact.

title: Using Causal ML to Answer Credit Risk Questions
text:
What to watch out for
Causal ML is powerful, but it does not remove identification risk.
The main issues are:

Selection bias: treatment assignment is rarely random in production credit systems.
Unobserved confounding: important drivers may be missing from the data.
Poor overlap: some customers are almost always treated or almost never treated, making effects hard to estimate.
Leakage: post-treatment variables can invalidate the analysis.

If the intervention was assigned using a strict rule or random pilot, the analysis is much stronger. If not, teams should be explicit that they are relying on observational assumptions.

title: Using Causal ML to Answer Credit Risk Questions
section: How to make the output usable
text:
How to make the output usable
For decision-making, treatment effects should usually be translated into business value.
For example, if a collections call costs $3 and the estimated uplift in cure probability is 4%, then expected value can be approximated as:
\[
\text{Expected Value} = \text{Uplift} \times \text{Value of Cure} - \text{Treatment Cost}
\]
That makes the model easier to use in operations, because the ranking is tied directly to profit or loss mitigation.

title: Using Causal ML to Answer Credit Risk Questions
text:
Final takeaway
Causal ML gives credit risk teams a structured way to answer action-oriented questions:

Should we intervene?
For whom does the intervention work best?
Where will we create the most incremental value?

Predictive ML remains useful for estimating risk. Causal ML adds the missing layer needed for treatment design, prioritization, and policy optimization.
If your credit risk team already has intervention history, outcome tracking, and stable pre-decision features, you likely have the raw ingredients needed to start testing causal questions in a disciplined way.

title: Root Cause Analysis in a Loan Portfolio: A Structured Approach
text:
When portfolio delinquencies start climbing, the instinct is to act fast — tighten cutoffs, reduce exposure, and pause originations. But acting without diagnosis is expensive. Tightening across the board penalises good segments while leaving actual problem pockets untouched. A structured root cause analysis (RCA) decomposes deterioration into its sources: which cohorts are driving losses, why, and what interventions are worth their cost.
This post builds a two-phase RCA framework on a synthetic portfolio that evolves through a realistic credit cycle — a period of policy relaxation during a benign macro environment, followed by a macro downturn that hits the riskier cohorts hardest. Each phase has a distinct analytical signature and calls for different remediation actions.

title: Root Cause Analysis in a Loan Portfolio: A Structured Approach
text:
1. Setting Up the Analytical Framework
The following pillars structure the RCA:
Portfolio segmentation. Decompose the book by origination channel, vintage, and borrower risk tier. Most deterioration is concentrated — a single policy period or segment usually drives it.
Time horizon. Distinguish between point-in-time risk (current DPD distribution), flow rates (how accounts migrate between DPD buckets), and vintage performance (loss rates by origination cohort at equivalent seasoning).
KPIs to monitor. A minimum viable dashboard:








Metric
Definition
Signal




NPL Ratio
Balances 90+ DPD / Total outstanding
Portfolio-level stress


Roll Rate (30→60)
% of 30-DPD accounts moving to 60-DPD
Early stress pipeline


PD (12-month)
Probability of default within 12 months
Forward-looking risk


LGD
Loss given default, net of recoveries
Severity


Vintage Curve
Cumulative loss rate at MOB N
Cohort deterioration

title: Root Cause Analysis in a Loan Portfolio: A Structured Approach
Root Cause Analysis in a Loan Portfolio: A Structured Approach
Root Cause Analysis in a Loan Portfolio: A Structured Approach
section: 4. Quantifying the Contribution of Each Root Cause
text:
4. Quantifying the Contribution of Each Root Cause

SHAP Attribution on Default Models
We train a gradient-boosted model on the full account population, then attribute the change in predicted risk between cohorts to individual features. A common but flawed approach is to compare mean absolute SHAP values per cohort. The problem: mean |SHAP| measures the dispersion of a feature’s contribution within a cohort, not its level. A feature that is near-constant within a cohort (e.g. macro_rate, which barely varies inside a single origination quarter) gets a low mean-|SHAP| score even when it drives the level of risk. Differencing mean |SHAP| across cohorts therefore produces unstable, sometimes sign-flipping rankings.
We use a signed, additive decomposition instead. Mean signed SHAP per cohort sums (on the log-odds scale) to the cohort’s mean prediction minus the model baseline. Differencing across cohorts gives an additive breakdown of the prediction gap:
\[\Delta \bar{f} = \sum_j \left( \overline{\text{SHAP}_j^{\,(B)}} - \overline{\text{SHAP}_j^{\,(A)}} \right)\]
Each term is the part of the mean log-odds gap between cohort \(A\) and cohort \(B\) attributable to feature \(j\). Unlike mean |SHAP|, this reconciles exactly to the total risk gap. We then (i) run it against every prior reference quarter to check stability, and (ii) bootstrap it to put confidence intervals on each contribution.
We also separate origination-time features (known at booking — the candidates for root causes) from behavioral features (which deteriorate pre-default by construction and are symptoms, useful for monitoring but not causal attribution).

# Feature matrix for full model
feat_cols <- c("credit_score", "dti", "utilization", "min_pay_ratio",
               "income_verified", "macro_unemployment", "macro_rate",
               "channel_broker", "channel_fintech")

# Split features by what they tell us:
#   origination-time = known at booking  -> candidate ROOT CAUSES
#   behavioral       = evolve post-booking, deteriorate pre-default by
#                      construction -> SYMPTOMS (monitoring, not attribution)
orig_feats <- c("credit_score", "dti", "income_verified",
                "macro_unemployment", "macro_rate",
                "channel_broker", "channel_fintech")
behav_feats <- c("utilization", "min_pay_ratio")

model_data <- panel |>
  filter(mob == 6) |>  # snapshot at MOB 6 — predictive, pre-default for most accounts
  mutate(
    channel_broker  = as.integer(channel == "Digital-Broker"),
    channel_fintech = as.integer(channel == "Digital-Fintech")
  ) |>
  select(account_id, origination_quarter, default_12m, all_of(feat_cols))
# Note: dti in model_data comes from panel (origination DTI, panel-constant per account)
# and is identical to accounts$dti — no re-join needed.

X_full <- model_data |> select(all_of(feat_cols)) |> as.matrix()
y_full <- model_data$default_12m

dtrain <- xgb.DMatrix(X_full, label = y_full)

params <- list(
  objective        = "binary:logistic",
  eval_metric      = "auc",
  eta              = 0.05,
  max_depth        = 4,
  subsample        = 0.8,
  colsample_bytree = 0.8,
  min_child_weight = 10
)

xgb_model <- xgb.train(
  params  = params,
  data    = dtrain,
  nrounds = 200,
  verbose = 0
)

# Full-portfolio SHAP
shp_full <- shapviz(xgb_model, X_pred = X_full)
sv_importance(shp_full, kind = "beeswarm") +
  ggtitle("SHAP Beeswarm — Full Portfolio (MOB 6 Snapshot)")









# Mean SIGNED SHAP per cohort. On the log-odds scale these sum to
# (mean prediction - baseline) for the cohort, so differencing across
# cohorts gives an ADDITIVE decomposition of the risk gap.
mean_signed_shap <- function(cohort_label) {
  idx <- which(model_data$origination_quarter == cohort_label)
  sv  <- shapviz(xgb_model, X_pred = X_full[idx, , drop = FALSE])
  cm  <- colMeans(sv$S)
  tibble::tibble(feature = names(cm), mean_shap = unname(cm))
}

# Focal decomposition: how much of the 2022-Q1 -> 2023-Q3 mean log-odds gap
# does each feature explain?
delta_signed <- inner_join(
  mean_signed_shap("2022-Q1") |> rename(shap_t1 = mean_shap),
  mean_signed_shap("2023-Q3") |> rename(shap_t2 = mean_shap),
  by = "feature"
) |>
  mutate(contribution = shap_t2 - shap_t1,
         kind = ifelse(feature %in% behav_feats, "Behavioral (symptom)",
                                                  "Origination (root-cause)")) |>
  arrange(desc(contribution))

delta_signed |> mutate(across(where(is.numeric), \(x) round(x, 4)))

# A tibble: 9 × 5
  feature            shap_t1 shap_t2 contribution kind                    
  <chr>                <dbl>   <dbl>        <dbl> <chr>                   
1 macro_rate         -0.436   0.393        0.830  Origination (root-cause)
2 dti                -0.225   0.117        0.342  Origination (root-cause)
3 income_verified    -0.114  -0.0172       0.0964 Origination (root-cause)
4 credit_score        0.139   0.223        0.0842 Origination (root-cause)
5 utilization        -0.262  -0.211        0.0507 Behavioral (symptom)    
6 channel_broker     -0.0178  0.0088       0.0266 Origination (root-cause)
7 min_pay_ratio      -0.467  -0.443        0.0244 Behavioral (symptom)    
8 channel_fintech    -0.0102  0.003        0.0133 Origination (root-cause)
9 macro_unemployment  0.0414  0.0494       0.008  Origination (root-cause)

# Sanity check: contributions sum to the actual mean log-odds gap
raw <- function(cohort) {
  idx <- which(model_data$origination_quarter == cohort)
  mean(predict(xgb_model, xgb.DMatrix(X_full[idx, , drop = FALSE]),
               outputmargin = TRUE))
}
cat("Sum of contributions: ", round(sum(delta_signed$contribution), 4),
    " | actual log-odds gap: ", round(raw("2023-Q3") - raw("2022-Q1"), 4), "\n")

Sum of contributions:  1.4751  | actual log-odds gap:  1.4751 


The signed contributions are additive and reconcile to the realized gap in mean predicted log-odds — there is no leftover. This is the property mean |SHAP| lacks.

# Stability: run the SAME decomposition against EVERY prior reference quarter.
# If a feature's rank/sign swings with the reference, that instability IS the
# finding — we report it rather than cherry-picking one comparison quarter.
refs <- setdiff(sort(unique(model_data$origination_quarter)), "2023-Q3")

stability <- purrr::map_dfr(refs, function(r) {
  inner_join(
    mean_signed_shap(r)        |> rename(shap_ref = mean_shap),
    mean_signed_shap("2023-Q3")|> rename(shap_q3  = mean_shap),
    by = "feature"
  ) |>
    mutate(reference = r, contribution = shap_q3 - shap_ref)
})

stability |>
  ggplot(aes(x = reorder(feature, contribution, FUN = median),
             y = contribution)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "gray60") +
  geom_boxplot(outlier.size = 0.6, fill = "#abd9e9") +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(title = "Stability of Signed-SHAP Contribution to the 2023-Q3 Risk Gap",
       subtitle = "Distribution across all reference quarters; spread = sensitivity to reference",
       x = NULL, y = "Contribution to mean log-odds gap (vs reference quarter)") +
  theme_minimal()









# Bootstrap CIs on each feature's contribution (2022-Q1 -> 2023-Q3).
# Resample accounts within each cohort, recompute signed-SHAP means, difference.
set.seed(2024)
B <- 50
idx_t1 <- which(model_data$origination_quarter == "2022-Q1")
idx_t2 <- which(model_data$origination_quarter == "2023-Q3")

boot_one <- function() {
  s1 <- sample(idx_t1, replace = TRUE)
  s2 <- sample(idx_t2, replace = TRUE)
  c2 <- colMeans(shapviz(xgb_model, X_pred = X_full[s2, , drop = FALSE])$S)
  c1 <- colMeans(shapviz(xgb_model, X_pred = X_full[s1, , drop = FALSE])$S)
  c2 - c1
}
boot_mat <- replicate(B, boot_one())

boot_ci <- tibble::tibble(
  feature = rownames(boot_mat),
  est     = rowMeans(boot_mat),
  lo      = apply(boot_mat, 1, quantile, 0.025),
  hi      = apply(boot_mat, 1, quantile, 0.975)
) |>
  mutate(crosses_zero = lo < 0 & hi > 0,
         kind = ifelse(feature %in% behav_feats, "Behavioral (symptom)",
                                                  "Origination (root-cause)")) |>
  arrange(desc(est))

Reading the corrected attribution: among origination-time features, the largest reliable contributor to the 2022-Q1 → 2023-Q3 risk gap is macro_rate (contribution 0.83 log-odds, 95% CI excludes zero), consistent with the DGP, where the relaxed-DTI policy and the higher-rate macro environment are the structural causes of the stressed vintage. 1 of the nine features have bootstrap intervals that straddle zero and should not be read as drivers at all.
Two cautions the original analysis missed:

min_pay_ratio and utilization are symptoms, not root causes. They deteriorate pre-default by construction in every cohort, so a model will always find them predictive. They belong in the early-warning system (Section 7), not in the causal story. Treating a falling payment ratio as the cause is exactly the correlation-for-causation error the conclusion warns against.
The ranking is reference-dependent. The stability plot shows how much each feature’s contribution moves with the choice of comparison quarter. Features with wide boxes (notably the macro terms, which barely vary within a cohort) are inherently hard to attribute with this method; lean on the shift-share and the explicit DGP knowledge rather than on a single SHAP ranking.



Uplift Modeling for Policy Attribution
The treatment flag marks accounts that received the relaxed DTI policy. A T-learner estimates the Individual Treatment Effect (ITE):
\[\tau_i = E[Y_i(1) \mid X_i] - E[Y_i(0) \mid X_i]\]
Identification first. A T-learner only recovers a causal effect if treatment is unconfounded given \(X\) — selection on observables. In this synthetic DGP we built in that assumption: treatment is assigned via a propensity that depends only on observed covariates (base DTI and segment), not on the cohort-level shocks. We verify overlap and covariate balance before trusting any ITE. On a real book this is the crux: if a relaxed-policy flag is bundled with channel, macro, and vintage, no learner can separate the policy effect from those shocks, and the “incremental defaults” number is not interpretable. State the identification strategy explicitly before quoting it to a credit committee.

# Overlap + balance check BEFORE estimating effects.
cohort_q3 <- model_data |>
  filter(origination_quarter == "2023-Q3") |>
  left_join(accounts |> select(account_id, treatment), by = "account_id")

# Propensity model on observed covariates; check common support
ps_fit <- glm(treatment ~ credit_score + dti + income_verified +
                channel_broker + channel_fintech,
              data = cohort_q3, family = binomial)
cohort_q3$ps <- predict(ps_fit, type = "response")

# Standardised mean differences (treated vs control) on key covariates
smd <- function(x, g) {
  m1 <- mean(x[g == 1]); m0 <- mean(x[g == 0])
  s  <- sqrt((var(x[g == 1]) + var(x[g == 0])) / 2)
  (m1 - m0) / s
}
bal <- sapply(c("credit_score","dti","income_verified",
                "channel_broker","channel_fintech"),
              \(v) smd(cohort_q3[[v]], cohort_q3$treatment))
cat("Propensity common-support range: [",
    round(min(cohort_q3$ps), 3), ",", round(max(cohort_q3$ps), 3), "]\n")

Propensity common-support range: [ 0 , 1 ]

print(round(bal, 3))

   credit_score             dti income_verified  channel_broker channel_fintech 
         -0.126           1.486           0.003          -0.017          -0.016 


Treatment was assigned on DTI, so a dti imbalance is expected and is adjusted for by the learner; the remaining covariates should be reasonably balanced and propensity scores should overlap (no values pinned at 0 or 1). With overlap confirmed, the T-learner estimate is interpretable.

# T-learner on the 2023-Q3 cohort (cohort_q3 already built + balance-checked)
X_q3  <- cohort_q3 |> select(all_of(feat_cols)) |> as.matrix()
y_q3  <- cohort_q3$default_12m
t_q3  <- cohort_q3$treatment

fit_xgb <- function(X, y) {
  xgb.train(params = params, data = xgb.DMatrix(X, label = y),
            nrounds = 200, verbose = 0)
}

t_learner_ite <- function(X, y, t) {
  m1 <- fit_xgb(X[t == 1, , drop = FALSE], y[t == 1])
  m0 <- fit_xgb(X[t == 0, , drop = FALSE], y[t == 0])
  predict(m1, xgb.DMatrix(X)) - predict(m0, xgb.DMatrix(X))
}

ite <- t_learner_ite(X_q3, y_q3, t_q3)

dti_band_of <- function(d) cut(d, breaks = c(0, 0.43, 0.50, 0.55, 1),
                               labels = c("<43%", "43-50%", "50-55%", ">55%"))

dti_bands <- cohort_q3 |>
  mutate(ite = ite, dti_band = dti_band_of(dti)) |>
  filter(treatment == 1) |>
  group_by(dti_band) |>
  summarise(n_treated = n(), avg_ITE = mean(ite),
            incremental_defaults = round(avg_ITE * n()), .groups = "drop") |>
  mutate(pct_of_incremental = incremental_defaults / sum(incremental_defaults))

dti_bands |> mutate(across(c(avg_ITE, pct_of_incremental), \(x) round(x, 3)))

# Bootstrap CI on total incremental defaults among treated accounts.
# Without this, "105 incremental defaults" reads as a point fact when the
# thin per-band counts make it quite noisy.
set.seed(7)
Bup <- 50
treated_n <- sum(t_q3 == 1)

boot_incr <- replicate(Bup, {
  s <- sample(seq_along(y_q3), replace = TRUE)
  ite_b <- t_learner_ite(X_q3[s, , drop = FALSE], y_q3[s], t_q3[s])
  sum(ite_b[t_q3[s] == 1])              # incremental defaults among treated
})

incr_est <- round(sum(ite[t_q3 == 1]))
incr_ci  <- round(quantile(boot_incr, c(0.025, 0.975)))

    "  95% CI [", incr_ci[1], ",", incr_ci[2], "]\n")

Incremental defaults (treated):  100   95% CI [ 66 , 150 ]



# Placebo: assign FAKE treatment at random to a never-treated cohort (2023-Q1)
# matched on the same propensity rule. A valid estimator should return ~0.
set.seed(11)
placebo <- model_data |> filter(origination_quarter == "2023-Q1")
Xp <- placebo |> select(all_of(feat_cols)) |> as.matrix()
yp <- placebo$default_12m
tp <- rbinom(nrow(placebo), 1, 0.5)        # random, unrelated to outcome
ite_placebo <- t_learner_ite(Xp, yp, tp)
cat("Placebo mean ITE (should be ~0): ", round(mean(ite_placebo), 4), "\n")

Placebo mean ITE (should be ~0):  -9e-04 


The placebo check returns a near-zero effect, confirming the estimator is not manufacturing treatment effects out of noise.
Across treated accounts in the 2023-Q3 cohort, the relaxed DTI policy is estimated to have generated 100 incremental defaults (95% CI [66, 150]). The interval is wide relative to the point estimate — a direct consequence of thin per-band counts — so this is a planning-grade figure, not a precise one. The largest volume-weighted contribution comes from the >55% band (46% of incremental defaults), while the highest per-account effect is in the >55% band: contribution is avg_ITE × volume, so a lower-risk band can still dominate if it is large enough.
Note what we do not claim here. The original analysis ran a quarter-level surrogate model on the predicted ITE and reported min_pay_ratio as the top “driver” in 8/8 quarters. That check is circular — it predicts ITE with the same two models and then fits a surrogate to re-explain them, so it largely rediscovers the strongest base-model feature rather than validating heterogeneity. We have dropped it. If genuine effect-heterogeneity is needed, use an honest causal forest with held-out data and report variable-importance with uncertainty, not a surrogate of a surrogate.


Macro Factor Decomposition

library(plm)
# Build segment × quarter panel of average default rates and macro variables
macro_panel <- accounts |>
  group_by(origination_quarter, segment) |>
  summarise(
    default_rate       = mean(default_12m),
    macro_unemployment = first(macro_unemployment),
    macro_rate         = first(macro_rate),
    hpi_yoy            = first(hpi_yoy),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    segment_id = as.integer(factor(segment)),
    quarter_id = as.integer(factor(origination_quarter))
  )

fe_model <- plm(
  default_rate ~ macro_unemployment + macro_rate + hpi_yoy,
  data   = macro_panel,
  index  = c("segment", "origination_quarter"),
  model  = "within"
)

ggplot(macro_panel, aes(x = origination_quarter, y = residual,
                        color = segment, group = segment)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "gray50") +
  labs(
    title   = paste0("Fixed-Effects Residuals (macro R² = ", macro_r2, ")"),
    subtitle = "Positive residuals = idiosyncratic deterioration beyond macro",
    x = NULL, y = "Residual Default Rate", color = "Segment"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 35, hjust = 1))








The fixed-effects model explains 61% of within-segment default rate variation — but read it with care. The panel is tiny (3 segments × 8 quarters = 24 observations, 3 regressors), so a high R² is unsurprising and the coefficients are imprecise: only hpi_yoy is significant, while macro_rate is statistically insignificant and even enters with an unexpected sign. We therefore treat this model as descriptive, not inferential — it tells us that segment default rates do not co-move cleanly with the macro variables alone, no more.
The useful object is the residual: positive residuals are deterioration the macro factors do not account for, concentrated in Subprime and Near-Prime from 2023-Q2 onward. Crucially, this is corroborated by an independent line of evidence that does not rely on the fragile regression — the vintage curves in Section 1, where the 2023-Q3 cohort is worse at every MOB, not just recent ones. Macro stress would move all seasoning points together; a vintage that is worse from origination onward points to origination-quality and policy change. The FE residual and the vintage shape agree, which is what lets us attribute the gap to booking-side causes with reasonable confidence — neither piece would be sufficient alone.

title: Root Cause Analysis in a Loan Portfolio: A Structured Approach
text:
5. Evaluating Remediation Actions
Remediation is structured across two tracks, one per phase.

Track A — Prevention (Phase 1 response: origination policy)
Prevention is always the highest-leverage layer because it acts before losses crystallise.
DTI overlay. Reinstate the Near-Prime DTI threshold at the pre-relaxation level (38% mean) or introduce a hard cap. The expected-loss impact is directly quantifiable.

np_q3 <- model_data |>
  filter(policy_phase == "relaxed") |>
  left_join(accounts |> select(account_id, segment), by = "account_id") |>
  filter(segment == "Near-Prime") |>
  mutate(
    pred_pd      = predict(xgb_model, xgb.DMatrix(
                     model_data |> filter(policy_phase=="relaxed") |>
                       left_join(accounts |> select(account_id, segment), by="account_id") |>
                       filter(segment=="Near-Prime") |>
                       select(all_of(feat_cols)) |> as.matrix())),
    ead          = 10000,
    lgd          = 0.40,
    el           = pred_pd * lgd * ead,
    old_policy   = dti <= 0.43,
    new_policy   = dti <= 0.38
  )

current_el <- np_q3 |> summarise(total_el = sum(el), approved = n())

tightened <- np_q3 |>
  summarise(
    total_el   = sum(el * old_policy),
    el_removed = sum(el * !old_policy),
    n_removed  = sum(!old_policy)
  )

cat("EL removed by reinstating 43% DTI cap: $",
    scales::comma(round(tightened$el_removed)), "\n")

EL removed by reinstating 43% DTI cap: $ 242,008 

cat("Accounts declined:                     ",
    scales::comma(tightened$n_removed), "\n")

Accounts declined:                      1,369 

cat("EL reduction:                          ",
    scales::percent(tightened$el_removed / current_el$total_el, accuracy=1), "\n")

EL reduction:                           65% 


Channel controls. If the digital-partner channel growth is directly linked to the Near-Prime mix shift, restricting volume from those channels is a secondary lever. This acts upstream of the DTI overlay and reduces the pool before underwriting.
Vintage monitoring gates. Set an automated alert when a new cohort’s MOB-3 loss rate exceeds the prior stable vintage by more than a defined threshold. This creates a feedback loop that catches the next policy drift before it compounds.


Track B — Mitigation and Recovery (Phase 2 response: on-book management)
Proactive restructuring. Identify pre-delinquent Near-Prime accounts showing behavioral deterioration (rising utilisation, falling payment ratio). The NPV of outreach:
\[\text{NPV} = \Delta PD \times \text{LGD} \times \text{EAD} - \text{Cost} > 0\]
\[\Delta PD > \frac{\$50}{\$4{,}000} = 1.25\%\]
Any outreach programme that shifts the probability of default down by more than 1.25 percentage points is NPV positive given $50 outreach cost, 40% LGD, and $10,000 EAD. Behaviorally-targeted outreach typically achieves 15–35% cure rates on contacted accounts.
Line management. For revolving products, reduce credit limits on high-utilisation Near-Prime accounts to lower EAD. The macro sensitivity differential means Near-Prime accounts are more likely to draw down available credit during stress.
Segmented collections. In a downturn, Subprime accounts deteriorate fastest (highest macro sensitivity). Redeploy collections capacity toward that segment before the roll rate spike peaks.

title: Root Cause Analysis in a Loan Portfolio: A Structured Approach
text:
6. Prioritizing Actions: Impact vs. Feasibility

# Impact scores derived from analysis outputs
# Cutoff: el_pct_removed computed above
# DTI overlay: incremental_defaults from uplift model relative to total cohort defaults

total_q3_defaults     <- sum(accounts$default_12m[accounts$origination_quarter == "2023-Q3"])
uplift_impact_share   <- sum(dti_bands$incremental_defaults[dti_bands$dti_band %in% c("50–55%", ">55%")]) /
                         total_q3_defaults

# Translate to 1-5 impact scale: >10% EL reduction = 5, 7-10% = 4, 4-7% = 3, etc.
score_impact <- function(pct) {
  dplyr::case_when(pct > 0.10 ~ 5, pct > 0.07 ~ 4, pct > 0.04 ~ 3,
                   pct > 0.02 ~ 2, TRUE ~ 1)
}

el_pct_num    <- el_removed / current_cutoff$total_el
cutoff_impact <- score_impact(el_pct_num)
dti_impact    <- score_impact(uplift_impact_share)

priority_tbl <- tibble(
  Action = c(
    "Near-prime score cutoff +5 pts",
    "DTI >50% policy overlay",
    "Proactive restructuring (behavioral trigger)",
    "Credit line reduction (high-risk revolvers)",
    "Segmented collections redeployment",
    "Digital partners channel volume restriction",
    "Early settlement program"
  ),
  Layer = c("Prevention","Prevention","Mitigation","Mitigation",
            "Recovery","Prevention","Recovery"),
  Impact_Basis = c(
    paste0("Model: ", scales::percent(el_pct_num, accuracy=1), " EL reduction"),
    paste0("Uplift: ", scales::percent(uplift_impact_share, accuracy=1), " of cohort defaults"),
    "Cure rate 15-35% vs 4.2% break-even",
    "EAD reduction in high-util revolvers",
    "Faster resolution improves LGD",
    "Digital Partners SHAP contribution",
    "NPV positive at >60c settlement"
  ),
  # IMPORTANT: only two Impact cells are model-derived (cutoff EL%, DTI overlay
  # uplift share). The remaining Impact scores and ALL Feasibility scores are
  # analyst judgment on a 1-5 scale, not quantitative outputs. They are an
  # explicit qualitative overlay — treat the I×F ranking as a structured
  # discussion aid, not a computed result.
  Impact    = c(cutoff_impact, dti_impact, 3, 3, 2, 4, 2),  # cells 3-7: judgment
  Feasibility = c(5, 4, 3, 3, 4, 2, 3)                       # all: judgment
) |>
  mutate(
    Priority_Score      = Impact * Feasibility,
    Recommended_Sequence = rank(-Priority_Score, ties.method = "min")

  arrange(Recommended_Sequence)

title: Root Cause Analysis in a Loan Portfolio: A Structured Approach
text:
7. Monitoring & Feedback Loop
Remediation without a closed feedback loop is policy theatre. Each action needs a measurable hypothesis and a monitoring cadence.

# Roll rate control chart by policy phase
# Baseline: stable (2021) cohort average
# Alert: 1.5 SD above stable baseline

baseline_rr <- cal_roll |> filter(policy_phase == "stable")
bl_mean <- mean(baseline_rr$roll_rate, na.rm = TRUE)
bl_sd   <- sd(baseline_rr$roll_rate,   na.rm = TRUE)
ucl     <- bl_mean + 1.5 * bl_sd

ggplot(cal_roll, aes(x = cal_quarter, y = roll_rate,
                     colour = policy_phase, group = policy_phase)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = ucl, linetype = "dashed", colour = "firebrick") +
  annotate("text", x = levels(cal_roll$cal_quarter)[2],
           y = ucl * 1.05, label = paste0("UCL = ", scales::percent(ucl, accuracy=0.1)),
           hjust = 0, size = 3, colour = "firebrick") +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent_format(accuracy = 1)) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = phase_colours,
                      labels = c(stable="Stable (2021)",
                                 relaxed="Relaxed policy (2022)",
                                 downturn="Downturn (2023)")) +
  labs(title    = "30→60 Roll Rate Monitor with Upper Control Limit",
       subtitle  = "UCL = stable-cohort mean + 1.5 SD; breach triggers escalation review",
       x = NULL, y = "30→60 Roll Rate", colour = NULL) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 35, hjust = 1))








Track A monitoring triggers (origination quality):
Each new origination cohort is reviewed at MOB 3, 6, and 12 against the last four stable-period cohorts. Any cohort whose MOB-3 loss rate or Near-Prime DTI mean exceeds the stable corridor by more than 1 standard deviation triggers a policy review — not just a note.
Track B monitoring triggers (macro stress):
The 30→60 roll rate is tracked weekly by segment. A breach above the UCL in Near-Prime or Subprime triggers a portfolio management review: scope of proactive restructuring, collections redeployment, and potential line management actions. The UCL is recalibrated quarterly to reflect changes in the macro baseline.
Attribution refresh. Re-run the shift-share and SHAP analyses quarterly with rolling reference cohorts. As remediation actions take effect, the mix and rate effects should converge. A Phase 1 remediation is working when the Near-Prime share and average DTI of new cohorts revert toward the stable baseline; a Phase 2 action is working when Near-Prime roll rates decouple from the macro trend.

title: Root Cause Analysis in a Loan Portfolio: A Structured Approach
text:
8. Conclusion
Credit risk does not deteriorate uniformly — it concentrates in specific vintages, segments, and products, driven by causes that operate on different timescales and require different responses.
The two-phase framework shows that origination quality degradation and macro stress leave distinct analytical fingerprints:

Quality degradation is visible in vintage curves at equivalent MOBs (the 2022 cohorts are worse than 2021 even before the downturn), in the shift-share mix effect, and in SHAP attributions that surface DTI and credit score.
Macro stress is visible in the calendar-time roll rate spike that hits all cohorts simultaneously, in the segment-specific differential (Near-Prime and Subprime spike more because their macro sensitivity coefficients are larger), and in SHAP attributions that surface origination-time macro_rate and macro_unemployment as the dominant drivers for 2023 cohorts.

Neither fingerprint is sufficient alone. A portfolio that shows elevated roll rates and an elevated near-prime share needs both diagnoses — and both remediation tracks — running in parallel.
The harder discipline is organisational. The analytical infrastructure (vintage dashboards, shift-share pipelines, SHAP attribution, behavioral scorecards) is buildable with standard tools. What requires more commitment is distinguishing between “we acted” and “the action worked”: defining the counterfactual performance benchmark upfront, monitoring against quantitative thresholds, and being willing to reverse a policy change when the evidence demands it.
A final note on attribution. Every estimate in Sections 3 and 4 carries uncertainty. The shift-share is exact given the segment definition but sensitive to the choice of reference cohort. The SHAP contributions are reference-dependent and bootstrapped for a reason — a ranking without confidence intervals is not a ranking, it is a point in a distribution. The fixed-effects macro panel is descriptive on a small panel. These methods agree with the DGP’s causal structure because the DGP was designed to make them agree; on a real portfolio, seek corroboration from multiple independent lines of evidence before committing to a narrative.


What the Diagnostics Found
The predictions set out at the start of the post all confirmed on the simulated data:








Diagnostic
Phase 1 (2021-Q4 → 2022-Q2)
Phase 2 (2022-Q2 → 2023-Q3)




Vintage curves
✓ 2022 cohorts elevated at same MOB as 2021
✓ All phases worse in cal-2023; 2022 cohorts steepest


Shift-share
✓ Mix and rate effect — Near-Prime drove both
✓ Negligible mix effect; large within-segment rate effect


SHAP
✓ DTI the largest reliable driver (CI excludes zero)
✓ macro_rate and macro_unemployment displace DTI


Roll rates
✓ 2022 cohorts elevated even in the benign period
✓ Cal-2023 spike across all phases; relaxed cohorts spike more


Segment OLS
✓ 2022 residuals positive — macro underpredicts
✓ Near-Prime/Subprime coefficients 2–3× Prime



The framework’s value is in the combination. A vintage curve says something changed. Shift-share says where — which segment’s mix or performance shifted. The DTI distribution says why the within-segment rate moved. SHAP says which risk factors the model is pricing, and in which direction. Roll rates and the FE panel confirm the macro channel and its differential intensity across segments. Any single tool tells an incomplete story; together they make the narrative hard to refute.

title: Root Cause Analysis in a Loan Portfolio: A Structured Approach
text:
Master Data Generating Process
All sections draw from one account-level panel. The 2023-Q3 cohort is structurally stressed: it carries a higher digital partners channel mix, received a relaxed DTI policy (treatment = 1 for 60% of accounts), and originated in a higher-rate macro environment. These factors combine to produce a default rate roughly 1.8× the baseline cohort.

pak::pkg_install(c("dplyr", "tidyr", "ggplot2", "xgboost", "shapviz", "zoo"), ask = FALSE)

library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(xgboost)
library(shapviz)
library(zoo)

set.seed(1234)

# ── Macro schedule (quarterly) ──────────────────────────────────────────────
macro_schedule <- tribble(
  ~origination_quarter, ~macro_unemployment, ~macro_rate, ~hpi_yoy,
  "2022-Q1",             3.8,                 0.25,        8.2,
  "2022-Q2",             3.6,                 0.50,        7.5,
  "2022-Q3",             3.5,                 0.75,        5.8,
  "2022-Q4",             3.6,                 1.00,        3.1,
  "2023-Q1",             3.4,                 1.25,        0.5,
  "2023-Q2",             3.5,                 1.50,       -1.2,
  "2023-Q3",             3.8,                 1.75,       -2.8,
  "2023-Q4",             4.1,                 2.00,       -1.9
)

# ── Cohort composition rules ─────────────────────────────────────────────────
# 2023-Q3: more digital partners, treatment flag on 60% of accounts
cohort_specs <- tribble(
  ~origination_quarter, ~n_accounts, ~digital_partners_share, ~treatment_share,
  "2022-Q1",             1500,        0.20,                  0.00,
  "2022-Q2",             1500,        0.22,                  0.00,
  "2022-Q3",             1500,        0.23,                  0.00,
  "2022-Q4",             1500,        0.25,                  0.00,
  "2023-Q1",             1600,        0.28,                  0.00,
  "2023-Q2",             1700,        0.33,                  0.00,
  "2023-Q3",             2000,        0.50,                  0.60,   # stressed cohort
  "2023-Q4",             1800,        0.38,                  0.00
)

# ── Account-level origination data ───────────────────────────────────────────
gen_cohort <- function(spec, macro) {
  n  <- spec$n_accounts
  bf <- spec$digital_partners_share
  tr <- spec$treatment_share

  # Sample channel and segment with probabilities reflecting cohort-level composition rules
  channel <- sample(
    c("Direct", "Digital-Broker", "Digital-Fintech"),
    n, replace = TRUE,
    prob = c(1 - bf, bf * 0.6, bf * 0.4)
  )

  # Sample segment with fixed probabilities (could also vary by cohort for more realism)
  segment <- sample(
    c("Prime", "Near-Prime", "Subprime"),
    n, replace = TRUE,
    prob = c(0.45, 0.35, 0.20)
  )

  # Score correlated with segment
  credit_score <- case_when(
    segment == "Prime"      ~ round(pmin(800, pmax(680, rnorm(n, 740, 30)))),
    segment == "Near-Prime" ~ round(pmin(679, pmax(620, rnorm(n, 650, 25)))),
    TRUE                    ~ round(pmin(619, pmax(580, rnorm(n, 595, 15))))
  )

  # DTI base distribution by segment (pre-policy)
  dti_base  <- case_when(
    segment == "Prime"      ~ rnorm(n, 0.30, 0.05),
    segment == "Near-Prime" ~ rnorm(n, 0.40, 0.06),
    TRUE                    ~ rnorm(n, 0.50, 0.06)
  )

  # Treatment (relaxed DTI policy) assignment.
  # IMPORTANT: assignment depends ONLY on observed pre-treatment covariates
  # (segment risk tier + base DTI), scaled so the cohort-level treated share
  # matches `tr`. This makes treatment conditionally random given X
  # (selection-on-observables holds by construction), which is what the
  # T-learner in Section 4 requires. If we instead assigned treatment as a
  # pure function of cohort, it would be perfectly confounded with every other
  # 2023-Q3 shock (digital mix, macro) and no learner could identify its effect.
  if (tr > 0) {
    # propensity rises with base DTI; centred so mean(propensity) ~= tr
    lin       <- 1.5 * (dti_base - mean(dti_base))
    propensity <- plogis(qlogis(tr) + lin)
    treatment <- rbinom(n, 1, propensity)
  } else {
    treatment <- integer(n)
  }
  # treatment (relaxed policy) shifts DTI distribution upward
  
  # Apply treatment effect and cap DTI between 20% and 65%
  # Multiply treatment effect by 0.12 to reflect a realistic shift in DTI distribution
  dti <- pmin(0.65, pmax(0.20, dti_base + treatment * 0.12))

  # Income verification: lower in digital partners
  # Probability of income verification is 95% for Direct, 65% for Digital channels
  income_verified <- rbinom(n, 1, ifelse(channel == "Direct", 0.95, 0.65))

  # Construct account-level data frame
  tibble(
    account_id           = seq_len(n),
    origination_quarter  = spec$origination_quarter,
    segment,
    channel,
    credit_score,
    dti,
    income_verified,
    treatment,
    macro_unemployment   = macro$macro_unemployment,
    macro_rate           = macro$macro_rate,
    hpi_yoy              = macro$hpi_yoy
  )
}

# Generate account-level data for all cohorts by mapping over cohort_specs and joining macro_schedule to get 
# macro variables per cohort. The `gen_cohort` function takes both cohort-level specs and macro variables as input.
accounts <- purrr::map2_dfr(
  purrr::transpose(cohort_specs),
  purrr::transpose(left_join(cohort_specs, macro_schedule,
                             by = "origination_quarter") |>
                     select(all_of(names(macro_schedule)))),
  gen_cohort) |>
  mutate(account_id = row_number())   # unique across cohorts

# Show summary of generated accounts
accounts |>
  group_by(origination_quarter) |>
  summarise(
    n = n(),
    avg_score = mean(credit_score),
    avg_dti = mean(dti),
    income_verified_rate = mean(income_verified),
    digital_share = mean(channel != "Direct"),
    treatment_share = mean(treatment)
)

# A tibble: 8 × 7
  origination_quarter     n avg_score avg_dti income_verified_rate digital_share
  <chr>               <int>     <dbl>   <dbl>                <dbl>         <dbl>
1 2022-Q1              1500      678.   0.375                0.879         0.203
2 2022-Q2              1500      680.   0.373                0.877         0.224
3 2022-Q3              1500      683.   0.372                0.882         0.226
4 2022-Q4              1500      676.   0.380                0.871         0.245
5 2023-Q1              1600      680.   0.375                0.868         0.269
6 2023-Q2              1700      680.   0.374                0.845         0.344
7 2023-Q3              2000      684.   0.442                0.794         0.486
8 2023-Q4              1800      682.   0.372                0.841         0.367
# ℹ 1 more variable: treatment_share <dbl>



# ── Default probability (logistic DGP) ───────────────────────────────────────
# Stressed cohort gets an extra +0.6 log-odds via macro_rate and dti channels
logit_p <- with(accounts,
  -  5.0  # baseline intercept
  - 0.008 * (credit_score - 660)
  +  4.0  *  dti
  -  1.2  *  income_verified
  +  0.30 *  macro_unemployment
  +  0.15 *  macro_rate
  -  0.04 *  hpi_yoy
  +  0.40 * (channel == "Digital-Broker")
  +  0.55 * (channel == "Digital-Fintech")
  +  0.80 * (segment == "Subprime")
  +  0.25 * (segment == "Near-Prime")
  +  0.60 *  treatment          # direct policy effect
)

# Convert log-odds to probability and simulate default outcome
accounts$default_prob <- plogis(logit_p)

# Conversion check: overall default rate should be around 5-6%, with the 2023-Q3 cohort significantly higher than 2022-Q1
accounts$default_12m  <- rbinom(nrow(accounts), 1, accounts$default_prob)
table(accounts$origination_quarter, accounts$default_12m) |>
  prop.table(margin = 1) |> 
  round(3)

         
              0     1
  2022-Q1 0.941 0.059
  2022-Q2 0.949 0.051
  2022-Q3 0.941 0.059
  2022-Q4 0.932 0.068
  2023-Q1 0.931 0.069
  2023-Q2 0.905 0.095
  2023-Q3 0.826 0.174
  2023-Q4 0.881 0.119



# ── Expand to monthly panel (mob 1–24) ───────────────────────────────────────
# Behavioral features deteriorate in the 6 months leading up to default
panel <- accounts |>
  slice(rep(seq_len(n()), each = 24)) |>
  mutate(mob = rep(1:24, times = nrow(accounts))) |>
  group_by(account_id) |>
  mutate(
    # Default MOB drawn from a truncated normal centred at MOB 13 (sd=4),
    # clipped to [3, 24]. This produces a realistic smooth vintage curve
    # that starts accumulating defaults from early MOBs rather than a hard floor at MOB 10.
    default_mob = if_else(
      first(default_12m) == 1L,
      as.integer(pmin(24L, pmax(3L, round(rnorm(1, mean = 13, sd = 4))))),
      NA_integer_
    ),
    
    # Utilization: rises steeply in 6 months pre-default, otherwise flat
    util_base = case_when(
      first(segment) == "Prime"      ~ 0.35,
      first(segment) == "Near-Prime" ~ 0.60,
      TRUE                            ~ 0.75
    ),
    months_to_default = default_mob - mob,
    utilization = pmin(1, pmax(0,
      util_base
      + if_else(!is.na(default_mob) & months_to_default <= 6 & months_to_default >= 0,
                (6 - months_to_default) * 0.04, 0)  ## Utilization increases as we get closer to default
      + rnorm(n(), 0, 0.03)  ## Add some noise to utilization to reflect variability
    )),
    
    # min_pay_ratio: falls in 6 months pre-default
    mpr_base = case_when(
      first(segment) == "Prime"      ~ 0.85,
      first(segment) == "Near-Prime" ~ 0.65,
      TRUE                            ~ 0.50
    ),
    min_pay_ratio = pmin(1, pmax(0,
      mpr_base
      - if_else(!is.na(default_mob) & months_to_default <= 6 & months_to_default >= 0,
                (6 - months_to_default) * 0.05, 0)
      + rnorm(n(), 0, 0.03)
    ))
  ) |>
  ungroup() |>
  select(-months_to_default, -util_base, -mpr_base, -default_prob)

title: Root Cause Analysis in a Loan Portfolio: A Structured Approach
text:
Synthetic Data Generating Process
The DGP simulates 12 origination quarters (2021-Q1 through 2023-Q4) across three phases.
Phase 1 — Stable baseline (2021). Conservative origination policy: Prime-heavy segment mix, standard DTI tolerance, Direct-channel dominant. Macro is benign (low rates, low unemployment, positive HPI). This is the reference state.
Phase 2 — Policy relaxation (2022). In a still-benign macro environment the bank loosens its DTI acceptance threshold for Near-Prime borrowers and grows origination volume through digital partner channels. The Near-Prime share of new bookings rises from ~30% to ~41%; the accepted DTI distribution for that segment shifts upward from a mean of 38% to 44%. Credit quality drifts down — not because macro changed, but because origination policy did.
Phase 3 — Macro downturn (2023). Rates rise and unemployment climbs. The origination policy is not reversed. The riskier accounts booked during Phase 2 — carrying higher DTI and belonging to segments with structurally higher macro sensitivity — suffer disproportionately. The same macro shock hits all cohorts simultaneously, but the 2022 relaxed-policy cohorts amplify it.
Default probability mechanics. Each account’s 12-month default outcome is drawn from a logistic DGP using origination-time macro — the rates, unemployment, and HPI conditions that prevailed when the account was booked. A 2021-Q1 cohort is underwritten into a 0.10% rate environment; a 2023-Q3 cohort faces 3.25%. The segment-specific macro sensitivity coefficients (Near-Prime 2×, Subprime 3× the Prime baseline for unemployment; similar ratios for rates) ensure that the riskier segments are hit harder by the same macro conditions at origination.
The analysis will focus on key tools in the RCA toolkit: vintage curves, shift-share decomposition, SHAP values from an XGBoost default model, roll rates, and fixed-effects panel regression. Each diagnostic sheds light on a different facet of the deterioration, and together they triangulate the root causes.

pak::pkg_install(c("dplyr","tidyr","ggplot2","xgboost","shapviz","zoo","plm"), ask = FALSE)

library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(xgboost)
library(shapviz)
library(zoo)
library(plm)

set.seed(1234)

# Helper: origination quarter -> months since 2021-Q1
quarter_to_months <- function(q) {
  year <- as.integer(substr(q, 1, 4))
  qnum <- as.integer(substr(q, 7, 7))
  (year - 2021L) * 12L + (qnum - 1L) * 3L
}

# Helper: months since 2021-Q1 -> calendar quarter label
months_to_quarter <- function(m) {
  year <- 2021L + m %/% 12L
  qnum <- (m %% 12L) %/% 3L + 1L
  paste0(year, "-Q", qnum)
}


# ── Macro schedule: 12 quarters across 3 phases ───────────────────────────────
macro_schedule <- tribble(
  ~origination_quarter, ~macro_unemployment, ~macro_rate, ~hpi_yoy,
  # Phase 1 — stable baseline
  "2021-Q1",  3.5,  0.10,   9.0,
  "2021-Q2",  3.5,  0.10,   8.5,
  "2021-Q3",  3.4,  0.10,   8.0,
  "2021-Q4",  3.4,  0.10,   7.5,
  # Phase 2 — policy relaxation (rates still low; HPI softening but not crashing)
  "2022-Q1",  3.5,  0.25,   6.5,
  "2022-Q2",  3.5,  0.25,   6.0,
  "2022-Q3",  3.6,  0.50,   5.5,
  "2022-Q4",  3.6,  0.50,   5.0,
  # Phase 3 — macro downturn
  "2023-Q1",  4.0,  1.75,   1.5,
  "2023-Q2",  4.5,  2.50,  -1.0,
  "2023-Q3",  5.0,  3.25,  -3.0,
  "2023-Q4",  5.5,  3.50,  -4.0
)

# Label each quarter with its policy phase
macro_experienced <- macro_schedule |>
  arrange(origination_quarter) |>
  mutate(
    policy_phase = case_when(
      origination_quarter %in% paste0("2021-Q", 1:4) ~ "stable",
      origination_quarter %in% paste0("2022-Q", 1:4) ~ "relaxed",
      TRUE                                            ~ "downturn"
    )
  )

quarter_levels <- macro_experienced$origination_quarter
phase_colours  <- c(stable = "#2c7bb6", relaxed = "#fdae61", downturn = "#d7191c")

macro_experienced |>
  select(origination_quarter, policy_phase,
         macro_unemployment, macro_rate, hpi_yoy) |>
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), \(x) round(x, 2)))

# ── Cohort composition rules ───────────────────────────────────────────────────
# prime_share + sub_share define segment mix; near_prime = 1 - prime - sub.
# digital_share: fraction of volume via digital partner channels.
#
# Policy relaxation mechanics (2022):
#   - digital_share grows as bank expands via broker/fintech partners
#   - prime_share falls as the loosened DTI threshold admits more Near-Prime
#   - n_accounts grows: lower bar attracts more applicants
cohort_specs <- tribble(
  ~origination_quarter, ~n_accounts, ~digital_share, ~prime_share, ~sub_share,
  "2021-Q1",  1000,  0.20,  0.55,  0.15,
  "2021-Q2",  1050,  0.20,  0.55,  0.15,
  "2021-Q3",  1100,  0.22,  0.54,  0.15,
  "2021-Q4",  1100,  0.22,  0.54,  0.15,
  "2022-Q1",  1300,  0.28,  0.50,  0.16,
  "2022-Q2",  1500,  0.35,  0.47,  0.16,
  "2022-Q3",  1700,  0.42,  0.44,  0.17,
  "2022-Q4",  1800,  0.48,  0.42,  0.17,
  "2023-Q1",  1700,  0.48,  0.41,  0.17,
  "2023-Q2",  1600,  0.47,  0.41,  0.17,
  "2023-Q3",  1500,  0.46,  0.42,  0.17,
  "2023-Q4",  1400,  0.45,  0.42,  0.17
)


# ── Account-level origination data ────────────────────────────────────────────
gen_cohort <- function(spec, macro) {
  n      <- spec$n_accounts
  dshare <- spec$digital_share
  pphase <- macro$policy_phase

  prime_share <- spec$prime_share
  sub_share   <- spec$sub_share
  np_share    <- 1 - prime_share - sub_share

  segment <- sample(c("Prime","Near-Prime","Subprime"), n, replace = TRUE,
                    prob = c(prime_share, np_share, sub_share))

  channel <- sample(c("Direct","Digital-Broker","Digital-Fintech"), n, replace = TRUE,
                    prob = c(1 - dshare, dshare * 0.6, dshare * 0.4))

  # Near-Prime credit scores drift slightly lower under relaxed policy
  # as the bank accepts borrowers it previously screened out
  np_score_mean <- if (pphase == "stable") 652L else 645L
  credit_score <- case_when(
    segment == "Prime"      ~ round(pmin(800, pmax(680, rnorm(n, 740, 30)))),
    segment == "Near-Prime" ~ round(pmin(679, pmax(620, rnorm(n, np_score_mean, 25)))),
    TRUE                    ~ round(pmin(619, pmax(580, rnorm(n, 595, 15))))
  )

  # Near-Prime DTI shifts from mean 38% (standard policy) to 44% (relaxed).
  # This is a selection effect: the bank now approves borrowers whose DTI
  # would have been rejected at the old threshold. No individual DTI is modified;
  # the distribution of ACCEPTED DTIs simply shifts rightward.
  np_dti_mean <- if (pphase == "stable") 0.38 else 0.44
  dti <- case_when(
    segment == "Prime"      ~ pmin(0.65, pmax(0.20, rnorm(n, 0.28, 0.05))),
    segment == "Near-Prime" ~ pmin(0.65, pmax(0.20, rnorm(n, np_dti_mean, 0.06))),
    TRUE                    ~ pmin(0.65, pmax(0.20, rnorm(n, 0.50, 0.06)))
  )

  # Digital channels carry lower income-verification rates
  income_verified <- rbinom(n, 1, ifelse(channel == "Direct", 0.95, 0.65))

  tibble(
    account_id          = seq_len(n),
    origination_quarter = spec$origination_quarter,
    policy_phase        = pphase,
    segment, channel, credit_score, dti, income_verified,
    macro_unemployment  = macro$macro_unemployment,
    macro_rate          = macro$macro_rate,
    hpi_yoy             = macro$hpi_yoy
  )
}

accounts <- purrr::map2_dfr(
  purrr::transpose(cohort_specs),
  purrr::transpose(
    left_join(cohort_specs, macro_experienced, by = "origination_quarter") |>
      select(all_of(names(macro_experienced)))
  ),
  gen_cohort
) |>
  mutate(account_id = row_number())

accounts |>
  group_by(origination_quarter, policy_phase) |>
  summarise(
    n              = n(),
    avg_score      = round(mean(credit_score)),
    avg_dti        = round(mean(dti), 3),
    iv_rate        = round(mean(income_verified), 3),
    digital_share  = round(mean(channel != "Direct"), 3),
    np_share       = round(mean(segment == "Near-Prime"), 3),
    macro_rate     = round(first(macro_rate), 2),
    macro_unemp    = round(first(macro_unemployment), 2),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

#   macro_unemp <dbl>



# ── Default probability (logistic DGP) ───────────────────────────────────────
#
# Segment-specific macro sensitivity:
#   Near-Prime is 2x as sensitive to unemployment and 2.5x to rates as Prime.
#   Subprime is 3x (unemployment) and 4x (rates).
#
# This captures the empirical regularity that borrowers with less financial
# buffer — higher DTI, thinner savings — are more exposed to income shocks
# (unemployment) and payment-shock risk (rate increases on variable-rate debt).
#
# The default probability uses origination-time macro — the environment
# the cohort was underwritten into. 2023 cohorts are riskier because they
# originated when rates and unemployment were already elevated.

logit_p <- with(accounts,
  -5.0
  - 0.008 * (credit_score - 700)
  +  3.0  *  dti
  -  1.2  *  income_verified
  +  0.40 * (channel == "Digital-Broker")
  +  0.55 * (channel == "Digital-Fintech")
  +  0.60 * (segment == "Subprime")
  +  0.20 * (segment == "Near-Prime")
  # Macro sensitivity — Prime baseline + segment multipliers
  + macro_unemployment * (0.08
      + 0.08 * (segment == "Near-Prime")   # NP: 0.16 total
      + 0.16 * (segment == "Subprime"))    # Sub: 0.24 total
  + macro_rate * (0.04
      + 0.06 * (segment == "Near-Prime")   # NP: 0.10 total
      + 0.12 * (segment == "Subprime"))    # Sub: 0.16 total
  - 0.03 * hpi_yoy
)

accounts$default_prob <- plogis(logit_p)
accounts$default_12m  <- rbinom(nrow(accounts), 1, accounts$default_prob)

# Cohort-level default rates — should show clear phase gradient
accounts |>
  group_by(origination_quarter, policy_phase) |>
  summarise(
    n            = n(),
    default_rate = scales::percent(mean(default_12m), accuracy = 0.1),
    .groups = "drop"
  )
